title: Lyra Biomed — On‑Prem Air‑Gapped Deployment Discovery
summary: Discovery focused on air-gapped on‑prem deployment for regulated clinical research workloads. Key requirements: no egress from cluster, offline/periodic update process, HSM/KMS integration for keys, SOC2/ISO artifacts, GPU hardware constraints (A100/NVLink), expected throughput/latency SLOs, and pilot timeline. Next steps: share security pack, offline installer checklist, BOM and pricing; schedule POC kick-off.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-02 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Ruiz (Lyra Biomed - Head of AI), Marco Silva (Lyra - IT Security), Priya Nair (Lyra - Infrastructure Lead)
---
[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, really excited to talk through Lyra's on‑prem requirements today. Quick intro—I'm Maya from Redwood, AE, and Samir our solutions engineer is here to cover technical stuff.
[00:00:12] Elena: Hi thanks, Elena here. We run a bunch of sensitive clinical NLP workflows, so looking at fully air‑gapped options.
[00:00:20] Marco: Marco from security, quick note, we can't allow any outbound connections from the inference cluster. All updates must be vetted and staged via our internal repo or removable media.
[00:00:33] Samir: Totally understood. We have a private on‑prem offering that supports air‑gapped installs. There are two main patterns—customer-managed image + offline installer or a vendor-supplied appliance that you host behind your firewall.
[00:00:45] Priya: We prefer a bring‑your‑own hardware model. We'll provision NVIDIA A100s in NVLink config, might be 4-card per node initially, could expand. Concern is runtime kernel compatibility and driver packaging for air‑gap.
[00:01:00] Samir: Right, drivers and CUDA stacks are usually the tricky bit. For the on‑prem package we provide an offline bundle that includes the runtime binaries, a tested CUDA driver bundle, and checksums. You install via our offline installer script that validates signatures.
[00:01:15] Elena: How do you handle secret keys? Our compliance team insists on HSM backing for any key material. We can't have plaintext keys on disk.
[00:01:23] Maya: We integrate with customer KMS/HSMs. For fully air‑gapped setups we support PKCS#11 HSMs and on‑prem Vaults — Samir can elaborate on the key rotation and retrieval flow.
[00:01:33] Samir: Yeah, the runtime speaks to a KMS shim locally; in air‑gapped mode it pulls wrapped keys that you unwrap with your HSM. There is no outbound to Redwood for keys. We store only an encrypted blob and metadata, and audit logs are shipped to your internal SIEM — or kept local depending on your policy.
[00:01:50] Marco: Audit logs need to be immutable and stored for 7 years per our regs, and we require tamper-evident storage. Does your agent support writing to a WORM (write once read many) store?
[00:02:00] Samir: We can configure log sinks to S3-compatible WORM storage or append-only file systems. The delivered package includes a log forwarder that supports configurable endpoints.
[00:02:10] Elena: Ok, on the model side, we plan to use a fine-tuned open model, maybe a quantized variant. We also want deterministic outputs for some evals — is there support for pinning seeds and deterministic runtimes?
[00:02:22] Samir: We support model pinning and deterministic modes. For quantization we recommend INT8 with nbits-aware kernels; determinism can vary slightly across kernels, but for evals you can pin a sequence length, seed, and use a fixed kernel set. There might be a small delta in floating point across driver versions.
[00:02:40] Priya: Another operational constraint — our datacenter doesn't allow internet access from racks; updates will be applied quarterly via a secure USB medium or internal artifact repository. How do you deliver patches?
[00:02:52] Maya: We provide signed offline bundles and a verifiable installer. For major patches you can stage them in a staging repo, run our preflight checks, and then push to prod. We also provide a checklist for validating rollout in air‑gapped networks.
[00:03:05] Marco: SLA question — if there's a critical security fix, what's the emergency process given we are air‑gapped?
[00:03:12] Samir: We have an emergency response runbook: we prepare a signed hotfix bundle, notify your security contact, and coordinate a manual transfer via your approved channel. That includes a verified checksum and a rollback package. For P0 incidents we can also support on‑site engineering if contract includes on‑prem support.
[00:03:30] Elena: Performance wise, our target is sub‑1200ms p99 for 512 token prompts for patient triage classification at 50 qps sustained. Is that feasible on our planned hardware?
[00:03:42] Samir: Rough estimate: A100 multi-node with batching and KV cache should hit that for smaller context lengths; 50 qps sustained depends on batching strategy and token mix. We can propose a config with dedicated reserved slots to keep latency predictable — ala Redwood Dedicated but run on‑prem.
[00:03:58] Maya: To add, we have smart routing and local caching techniques to reduce repeated prefix compute. In air‑gapped mode caching still works fully local.
[00:04:08] Marco: Data residency — all inference logs and prompts must remain in scope of our on‑prem storage and never leave. Is there any telemetry that leaves the box by default?
[00:04:18] Samir: No telemetry leaves the box in air‑gapped configuration. Our standard hosted offering collects anonymized telemetry, but the private package disables outbound telemetry and all analytics write to local stores only.
[00:04:28] Priya: What about license and attestations? We need software bill of materials (SBOM), third‑party license list, and provenance for model weights.
[00:04:36] Maya: We supply SBOMs and third‑party notices as part of the security pack. For model provenance we include checksums and model lineage metadata; if you need an attestation we can create one with signatures.
[00:04:47] Elena: Any known limitations with air‑gap? For instance, auto-scaling features or burst capacity?
[00:04:54] Samir: Autoscaling is constrained—you won't have Redwood-managed burst pools since those rely on cloud connectivity. We support local autoscaling within the cluster using your node pool. For burst beyond that we'd need a dedicated co-lo or a temporary outbound-approved window, which I know is not ideal.
[00:05:08] Maya: Many customers accept local autoscaling policies combined with capacity planning and scheduling.
[00:05:14] Marco: We're hoping for a predictable pricing model — what are the options? CAPEX for hardware plus Redwood annual license or one-time perpetual plus support?
[00:05:22] Maya: We can do subscription/license models: annual support + software subscription for the private package, or an enterprise perpetual with annual maintenance. We'll cut a pricing sheet based on your expected node counts.
[00:05:32] Elena: Pilot scope — we'd like a 4‑week POC validating throughput and latency with one model family, plus security and offline update test. Does Redwood do that?
[00:05:40] Samir: Yes, we typically do a 4–6 week POC. For air‑gapped we run a joint playbook — hardware validation, offline install, a small benchmark harness, and a security audit.
[00:05:52] Priya: Can you run a benchmark harness against our internal dataset without sending data out?
[00:05:58] Samir: Absolutely, the harness runs locally. We'll bring the harness as a container you run inside your cluster and it outputs results to local storage. We can also produce a redacted summary for Redwood if you permit.
[00:06:10] Marco: About encryption at rest — we use LUKS on disks and we also have HSM unsealing at boot. Does the Redwood package play with the boot-time unseal?
[00:06:19] Samir: Yes, we've deployed with LUKS and HSM unseal flows. Our services expect to be started after the nodes are unsealed; the installer can hook into your boot processes.
[00:06:28] Maya: Quick note on support levels: we have premium on‑call SRE support as an add‑on for on‑prem customers for 24/7 coverage and remote/onsite support.
[00:06:36] Elena: Great. A few nitty things — do you support SAML SSO for the admin console and RBAC scoped to teams?
[00:06:43] Samir: Yes, SAML/SSO and LDAP integration for RBAC are supported. Admin console can be run off-cluster and the auth talks to your IdP over the internal network.
[00:06:53] Priya: We need to validate GPU driver versions. Which driver versions are in your published offline bundle?
[00:06:58] Samir: We'll publish tested driver bundles for specific CUDA versions — we target NVIDIA driver 525+ and CUDA 11/12 tested combinations. We'll include a compatibility matrix in the BOM.
[00:07:08] Marco: On legal — do you provide a data processing addendum that explicitly states no data exfiltration and liability terms for air‑gapped deployments?
[00:07:16] Maya: Yes, we have a DPA and can add contract language for air‑gapped deployments; legal is used to negotiated language for on‑prem.
[00:07:24] Elena: Ok, timeline — we're aiming to start a pilot mid‑April. Is that realistic?
[00:07:29] Maya: If we get hardware procurement confirmed this week and you share network diagrams, we can target a mid‑April kick off. That lines up with a 4‑week POC finishing mid‑May.
[00:07:40] Priya: I'll need to share network diagrams and procurement ETA — I can get that by next Monday.
[00:07:46] Marco: I'll also need the SOC2 and SBOM before legal greenlights anything.
[00:07:51] Maya: We'll package and send the security pack and SOC2 attestation tomorrow. Samir will prepare the offline installer checklist and BOM.
[00:07:59] Samir: I'll include a recommended node configuration for the A100 NVLink 4‑GPU layout and an alternate lower-cost config for the POC.
[00:08:08] Elena: Good. A few clarifying questions from my team: 1) Can we pin model versions and prevent automatic model upgrades? 2) How do you handle model weight redistribution if a vulnerability is discovered?
[00:08:20] Samir: 1) Yes, models are pinned. No automatic upgrades in private on‑prem; upgrades are manual and signed. 2) If a vulnerability in a model is discovered, we produce a patched model artifact and the roll‑out is manual in air‑gapped installs. We also provide a rollback artifact for safe reversion.
[00:08:36] Priya: About packaging — do you deliver as RPMs/Debs or a container image? Our infra team prefers containers to avoid host package changes.
[00:08:44] Samir: We provide both: container images for runtime and optional host packages for low-level driver helpers. The offline bundle contains images and a container registry tarball for import into your internal registry.
[00:08:58] Maya: Great questions. I want to make sure we capture action items and next steps before close.
[00:09:05] Elena: Sounds good.
[00:09:10] Maya: Recap: Redwood will send security pack (SOC2, SBOM), offline installer checklist, BOM with recommended node configs, and a draft SOW for a 4‑week POC. Lyra will share network diagrams, procurement timeline, and POC success criteria. Proposed POC kick off mid‑April.
[00:09:27] Marco: That matches. Also please include the emergency hotfix runbook in the security pack.
[00:09:33] Samir: Yep will include that.
[00:09:36] Priya: One more: can you include an estimated licensing cost ballpark so we can budget? Even a notional number helps.
[00:09:42] Maya: We'll include a ballpark pricing sheet — subscription vs perpetual options.
[00:09:47] Elena: Ok thanks everyone.
[00:09:50] Maya: Thank you, we'll follow up with materials by end of day tomorrow and schedule the POC kickoff once we have hardware dates.
[00:09:58] Marco: Thanks all.
[00:10:00] (call ends)
